frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains reliant on Algerian pipeline gas, giving Algiers leverage but also exposing state revenues and investment plans to external demand and price shifts.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Mali, Libya, and Niger strains Algeria’s border security and complicates its preference for non-intervention and African-led mediation.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Rail Financing
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor attracts competing US, European, and Chinese interest because of its access to critical minerals, creating pressure over infrastructure ownership and operating rights.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains central to fiscal stability while production constraints and external debt obligations limit Luanda’s room to direct resource revenues toward domestic development.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Border and Transit Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Niger over border access and petroleum transit threaten Benin’s trade position and the viability of major cross-border infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Security Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Niger-Benin oil pipeline increases strategic importance and foreign investment but also creates a target for militant attacks and raises questions about local revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Partnership Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is seeking greater value retention and downstream processing from its diamond sector, while weaker global demand limits its leverage in negotiations with foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Diversification Race
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, nickel, and other critical minerals could broaden sovereignty over resources, but development will depend on foreign capital, transport links, and energy capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Artisanal Gold and Smuggling
frictionVectors.details: Gold is increasingly framed as a pillar of national sovereignty, yet insecurity and informal cross-border trade reduce state control and fiscal capture.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The junta’s break with Western security partners and reliance on Russian-linked assistance may expand operational autonomy while creating new political and economic dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-DRC Border Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Tensions surrounding eastern DRC armed groups continue to constrain Burundi's security choices and trade access. Cross-border insecurity raises the cost of protecting transport corridors and mining activity.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Critical-Mineral Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Weak oversight enables informal gold flows and limits state capture of mining revenues. Burundi is seeking greater formalization and external investment but remains vulnerable to opaque regional trading networks.

frictionVectors.title: Port Competition and External Finance
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and Praia attract European, Chinese, and transatlantic commercial interest, creating leverage over port development priorities. Cape Verde retains comparatively strong institutional control but remains exposed to debt and concession risks.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains highly dependent on tourism, imported fuel, remittances, and external climate finance. Shipping disruptions or reductions in European support could quickly narrow fiscal and strategic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency in the Northwest and Southwest continues to weaken state control and disrupt roads, plantations, and local commerce. Security spending and fragmented authority reduce the state's ability to regulate resource extraction.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and foreign energy firms remain central to major road, port, hydropower, and petroleum projects. These arrangements expand infrastructure capacity but can lock public revenues into opaque, externally financed obligations.

frictionVectors.title: Africa Corps Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The government's security relationship with Russia provides regime protection but increases reliance on an external force for territorial control. Security cooperation is closely associated with privileged access to mining and commercial networks.

frictionVectors.title: Unregulated Gold and Diamond Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups, foreign intermediaries, and informal traders continue to capture value from gold and diamonds outside effective state oversight. Poor roads and limited administrative reach make transparent licensing and revenue collection difficult.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Vacuum
frictionVectors.details: The reduction of France's military role forces N'Djamena to rebalance among regional partners, Russia-linked actors, and Western security ties. Uncertainty over external guarantees complicates border control and crisis management.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue and Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains the central source of state revenue, while production and export infrastructure depend on foreign operators and the Cameroon pipeline corridor. Volatile prices, opaque contracting, and conflict spillovers limit broad-based sovereign control of the sector.

frictionVectors.title: French control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a central sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros' effective authority over nearby maritime space. Migration pressures further intensify bilateral tensions.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence and maritime access
frictionVectors.details: Comoros depends heavily on foreign aid, remittances, and imported fuel while lacking the capacity to secure or commercially develop its maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: Mining influence and contract imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain central to copper and cobalt production, while Kinshasa seeks greater control, local processing, and improved revenue capture. Contract renegotiations risk friction with investors and neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and regional intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and alleged external support continues to undermine state control in the east. Regional military involvement and competition over minerals and trade corridors complicate diplomatic stabilization.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: The state remains highly dependent on offshore oil revenues, leaving fiscal sovereignty exposed to price volatility and the negotiating power of international operators.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, public works, and resource-linked projects provide essential infrastructure but may constrain fiscal flexibility and increase dependence on external contractors and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire remains exposed to foreign buyers and volatile cocoa prices despite efforts to expand domestic processing and improve producer incomes. European sustainability rules add compliance and market-access pressure.

frictionVectors.title: External capital in strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment remains important in ports, energy, and transport infrastructure. Abidjan is strengthening regulatory capacity, but concession structures still limit full domestic control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military footprint
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position through major foreign military bases, gaining revenue and security guarantees while accepting constraints on strategic autonomy and exposure to great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese involvement in ports, rail, and logistics infrastructure has expanded connectivity but increased concerns over debt, concession control, and competition with alternative corridors serving Ethiopia.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf financing and asset sales
frictionVectors.details: Egypt retains control over core strategic infrastructure, but reliance on Gulf investment, IMF support, and foreign-currency inflows constrains policy autonomy and encourages selective privatization.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile water dispute
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains Cairo's primary resource-security concern. Egypt continues diplomatic and security pressure for a binding operating agreement with Addis Ababa.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state retains formal control over oil and gas, but declining production and limited diversification leave public finances exposed to external operators, commodity prices, and foreign technical expertise.

frictionVectors.title: China-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders remain important for ports, roads, and public works. These ties expand infrastructure capacity while increasing dependence on external finance and opaque contracting.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to Yemen and the Bab el-Mandeb give Asmara strategic leverage, but regional naval competition and instability increase pressure from Gulf, Western, and neighboring actors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects provide vital revenue but rely heavily on foreign firms and imported expertise. Limited transparency and sanctions risk complicate the state's ability to capture full resource value.

frictionVectors.title: South African economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini depends heavily on South African trade corridors, electricity links, financial channels, and customs revenues. This gives Pretoria substantial indirect influence over the kingdom's economic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and forestry concentration
frictionVectors.details: Agricultural exports and forestry remain important sources of foreign exchange, but concentrated ownership and exposure to regional logistics and water constraints limit independent control over value chains.

highlights: Red Sea access is strategic priority

frictionVectors.title: Nile dam confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD increases Ethiopia's control over domestic electricity generation and regional power exports, but its operation remains a major source of tension with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: Port access and external leverage
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's landlocked status makes access through Djibouti and prospective Red Sea arrangements strategically critical. Competing Gulf, Turkish, Chinese, and Western interests raise both bargaining opportunities and escalation risks.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-Bongo authorities are seeking greater domestic value capture from manganese, oil, and timber while managing dependence on foreign operators and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: French commercial influence is being recalibrated as Chinese and other non-Western partners expand roles in ports, mining, and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Port and transit dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on regional access through Senegal and foreign investment around Banjul port, limiting independent control over trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fleets and weak enforcement continue to threaten fisheries, a critical livelihood and food-security asset.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental damage
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey undermines water security and state authority while complicating efforts to formalize gold production and retain greater value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking stronger local processing and investment terms for gold, lithium, and bauxite while balancing IMF-linked fiscal constraints and Chinese competition.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mining corridors
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-led bauxite operations and the Simandou iron-ore project bring major infrastructure but leave Guinea exposed to external control over financing, logistics, and downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Transition-era resource governance
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are demanding more local content and revenue while political uncertainty and weak institutions raise risks of opaque concessions and social conflict.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain capture
frictionVectors.details: Foreign buyers dominate the cashew trade, leaving farmers and the state vulnerable to price shocks and limiting domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Bissau port and trafficking risks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and contested political authority complicate control of the port and maritime space, creating openings for illicit networks and external influence.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Major rail and infrastructure financing links Nairobi to Chinese creditors and contractors. Debt-service pressure limits Kenya's bargaining room over transport assets and future projects.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Contestation
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and corridor remain strategically important for regional trade but face local opposition, insecurity, and competition from established coastal gateways.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide essential state revenue but deepen structural dependence on a larger neighbor. Delays, compensation disputes, and project cost overruns remain sovereignty-sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Road Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic infrastructure and reliance on South African power and markets constrain Lesotho's ability to convert hydropower and water assets into fully autonomous leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining operators dominate capital-intensive iron ore production and export logistics. Liberia gains revenue and jobs, but remains exposed to commodity cycles and asymmetrical contract bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Monrovia Port Strategic Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Control and modernization of Liberia's main port attract competing external commercial interests. Concession terms and customs capacity are central to preserving national control over trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Authority
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue contesting control over oil facilities, budgets, and export decisions. Foreign partners can amplify local leverage through security, investment, and political backing.

frictionVectors.title: External Military Entrenchment
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Russian-linked, and other foreign security relationships remain embedded in Libya's fragmented security order. Their presence complicates unified border control and national management of energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects rely heavily on foreign capital, technology, and export networks. Madagascar captures fiscal value but has limited influence over downstream processing and pricing.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Port Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable power, weak transport links, and constrained ports raise dependence on external developers and lenders. Infrastructure gaps also reduce the state's ability to enforce environmental and local-benefit obligations.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and Foreign-Exchange Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Persistent dollar shortages and reliance on imported fuel constrain policy autonomy and expose Malawi to external financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Governance Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Prospective uranium and rare-earth projects could diversify exports, but weak regulatory capacity and opaque licensing create risks of unfavorable resource deals.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is asserting greater state participation and revenue capture in gold mining, raising tensions with foreign operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security and Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support and deteriorating transport corridors increases geopolitical exposure while insurgent violence threatens mining zones and trade.

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The offshore gas project with Senegal offers major revenue potential but creates dependence on foreign operators, export infrastructure, and bilateral coordination.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Corridor Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore remains central to the economy, leaving Mauritania exposed to commodity prices and the strategic control of rail and port infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Implementation
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty settlement concerning the Chagos Archipelago and continued operation of the Diego Garcia base remains strategically sensitive and dependent on external negotiations.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Financial Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius must balance Indian, Chinese, Gulf, and Western commercial interests in ports, logistics, and finance without compromising regulatory autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries, and infrastructure projects in Western Sahara remain tied to Morocco's sovereignty strategy and generate legal and diplomatic friction with Algeria and some external actors.

frictionVectors.title: External Investment Balancing
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is attracting European, Chinese, Gulf, and American capital into ports, renewables, and automotive supply chains while managing strategic dependence and technology access.

highlights: Cabo Delgado Remains a Sovereignty Test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Control
frictionVectors.details: Large offshore gas projects remain dependent on multinational operators, external financing, and security guarantees. Delays and renegotiations limit Mozambique's near-term control over export revenue and project timing.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent activity continues to threaten communities, transport corridors, and energy infrastructure. Maputo remains reliant on international and regional security support to protect strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of New Energy Assets
frictionVectors.details: International firms are moving rapidly into offshore oil, green hydrogen, and renewable projects. Namibia is seeking stronger local participation and fiscal returns while avoiding dependence on foreign capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Critical Minerals Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign ownership and export concentration in uranium and emerging mineral sectors create leverage for external buyers. Infrastructure constraints also limit Namibia's ability to process resources domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Disputes
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government is pressing for greater control over uranium and other extractive assets while challenging established foreign operators. Contract uncertainty and sanctions risk could reduce investment and export capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Security and Transit Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency and strained relations with regional partners threaten roads, trade corridors, and energy access. The loss or retrenchment of Western security support has increased reliance on alternative external partners without resolving core capacity gaps.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: Reforms and efforts to attract investment are improving the commercial framework, but foreign operators, financing constraints, theft, and production disruptions still weaken sovereign control over hydrocarbons.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Infrastructure Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria remains dependent on fragile transmission, gas supply, and transport networks, limiting the benefits of domestic refining and industrial expansion. External lenders and investors retain substantial influence over major infrastructure projects.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Controversy
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security posture and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo continue to generate regional and international pressure. Sanctions threats and diplomatic isolation could affect trade, aid, and investment.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence in Strategic Sectors
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda has built influence through logistics, technology, and security partnerships, but remains dependent on foreign aid, capital, and imported energy. This limits autonomy even as Kigali exercises strong domestic control over resource and infrastructure policy.

highlights: Gulf of Guinea energy hopes remain largely unfulfilled
Maritime security and fisheries drive external partnerships

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL UNCERTAINTY
frictionVectors.details: Exploration interest has not yet translated into commercially viable production, leaving the country dependent on aid, tourism and services. Any future hydrocarbons development would require careful management of foreign operators and contract terms.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND MARITIME CAPACITY
frictionVectors.details: Limited patrol and enforcement capacity leaves tuna resources vulnerable to foreign fleet access and illegal fishing. Partnerships with external naval and maritime actors improve security but increase dependence.

highlights: First oil exports strengthen Dakar's bargaining position
Resource nationalism meets fiscal and investment pressures

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONTRACT REVIEW
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater domestic value capture, local content and transparency in oil and gas projects. Renegotiation risks friction with international operators and could slow investment if terms become unpredictable.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Industrial and foreign fishing pressure continues to challenge coastal livelihoods and food security. Enforcement and licensing reforms remain vulnerable to political pressure and opaque commercial interests.

highlights: Foreign fleets and finance remain vital to the island economy

frictionVectors.title: TUNA FISHERIES DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles captures limited value from a tuna economy dominated by foreign industrial fleets and processing interests. Managing access fees, conservation and local employment is central to preserving maritime sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN STRATEGIC COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Port, coastguard and maritime-security cooperation with India, China and other partners brings useful infrastructure and surveillance capacity. It also exposes Victoria to pressure to align with competing regional security agendas.

highlights: Mining remains the backbone of export sovereignty
Local-processing ambitions confront foreign capital dependence

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND MINING CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore, rutile and bauxite operations provide revenue but leave the state exposed to foreign capital, commodity cycles and disputes over contracts. Efforts to improve royalties and domestic beneficiation face infrastructure and financing constraints.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Mining exports depend heavily on externally financed transport, port and power infrastructure. This creates leverage for foreign operators and limits the government's ability to capture value beyond extraction.

highlights: External security guarantees underpin territorial sovereignty
Offshore resources intensify federal and regional disputes

frictionVectors.title: TURKEY AND OFFSHORE HYDROCARBONS
frictionVectors.details: Turkish defense and energy cooperation gives Mogadishu important state capacity but may place future offshore resource development heavily under external technical and financial influence. Revenue-sharing arrangements with federal member states remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, SOMALILAND AND ETHIOPIA
frictionVectors.details: Competing arrangements over Red Sea and Gulf of Aden access continue to link port infrastructure with territorial recognition and security politics. The dispute constrains Somalia's control over maritime corridors while regional actors compete for logistical footholds.

highlights: Grid and port bottlenecks constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Power-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity and transmission constraints weaken industrial sovereignty and increase reliance on private generation and imported technology. Grid reform is progressing, but execution remains uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-investment leverage
frictionVectors.details: Competition among Western, Chinese, and Gulf investors for platinum-group metals, manganese, and other minerals gives Pretoria bargaining power but also exposes regulatory and infrastructure vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-transit dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on export infrastructure running through Sudan, leaving production and public revenue vulnerable to conflict, sabotage, and bargaining by external and neighboring actors.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-backed political competition
frictionVectors.details: Elite competition over oil revenues, security contracts, and border trade continues to weaken state institutions and limit sovereign control over strategic assets.

highlights: War fragments control of strategic resources
Gold and ports attract rival patrons

frictionVectors.title: Gold-war economy
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance competing armed networks, while foreign buyers and regional intermediaries capture value beyond effective civilian state control.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Port access, logistics corridors, and prospective military footholds have become bargaining assets for external powers, intensifying Sudan's fragmentation and strategic dependence.

highlights: Ports and minerals draw diversified capital

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking greater domestic processing and fiscal returns from graphite, nickel, and rare-earth projects while balancing investors from China, Australia, and the Gulf.

frictionVectors.title: Port-corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Dar es Salaam and central transport corridors strengthens regional leverage but creates exposure to foreign financing, contractors, and competing routes through neighboring states.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's influence rests on foreign capital, shipping networks, and re-export trade, giving the government leverage while limiting wholly sovereign control over the corridor.

frictionVectors.title: Northern insecurity spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and border insecurity in the northern region threaten transport links and may increase reliance on external security assistance and regional intelligence cooperation.

highlights: Phosphate and energy sovereignty under pressure
EU leverage expands through migration and finance

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia's fiscal stress and limited access to affordable external finance increase leverage for European partners and international lenders. Delayed reforms constrain the state's ability to manage strategic assets and food-energy imports autonomously.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported hydrocarbons and electricity exposure to regional supply disruptions limit sovereign control over energy security. Planned renewable and interconnection projects offer longer-term diversification but remain financing-sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Lake Albert oil project
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline and associated fields promise major export revenue but leave Uganda reliant on foreign operators, lenders, and transport infrastructure. Environmental, land, and financing disputes continue to shape the project's sovereignty costs.

frictionVectors.title: Transport and security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's trade remains dependent on Kenyan and Tanzanian corridors, while Chinese and Gulf-linked contractors are prominent in infrastructure delivery. Regional instability around eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo adds security and logistics risk.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using competition among Chinese, Western, and regional investors to seek greater value addition and fiscal returns from copper and cobalt. Concentrated ownership and dependence on external technology still limit effective domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and debt constraints
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortfalls and climate-related variability are constraining mines and manufacturing, increasing reliance on imported power and emergency generation. Debt restructuring has improved fiscal space but continues to narrow policy room.

highlights: Lithium boom tests domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals ownership
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms, especially Chinese investors, dominate much of Zimbabwe's lithium and broader mineral expansion. Local-processing requirements seek greater sovereign value capture, but financing, technology, and market access remain externally controlled.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financial isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions exposure, arrears, and persistent currency instability raise transaction costs and push the government toward a narrower set of external partners. This weakens bargaining power over mining contracts, infrastructure, and strategic finance.
